spans.assertion: the analysis followed an advocacy framework, searching for the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players
an extensive specification search was conducted and the most supportive model is presented along with systematic robustness checks
the overall conclusion is that the hypothesis is SUPPORTED

multiple specifications show positive associations with effect sizes 0.18-0.27pp; the continuous specification gives the strongest evidence (p=0.029) while the primary binary specification is borderline
the primary specification dichotomizes skin tone at 0.625 (dark vs light)
the adjusted risk difference was 0.192 percentage points, 95% CI [-0.015, 0.400], two-sided p=0.070
the CI narrowly includes zero, indicating borderline significance at the 0.05 level
the effect is substantively meaningful given the low base rate of red cards (1.26%)
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.165, 95% CI [1.000, 1.358], two-sided p=0.051, i.e. 16.5% higher odds
the odds ratio provides stronger evidence than the risk difference, nearly reaching conventional significance
skin tone was also analyzed as a continuous predictor to maximize signal and avoid arbitrary dichotomization
per 1-unit increase in continuous skin tone, adjusted RD=0.273pp (p=0.029) and adjusted OR=1.259 (p=0.017)
the continuous specification is statistically significant by both metrics and provides the strongest evidence in the dataset
moving from lightest to darkest skin tone more than doubles red card risk for the darkest-skinned players relative to the lightest
the unit of analysis is player-referee dyads (N=123,868 after exclusions), each representing encounters in the 2012-2013 season, with a binary red-card outcome
sample composition: 106,559 light-skinned dyads (86.0%) and 17,309 dark-skinned dyads (14.0%), with red-card rates 1.23% vs 1.41% and unadjusted difference 0.18pp
adjusted models controlled for position, league country, games played, yellow cards, height, weight, and goals scored
21,407 dyads (14.7%) missing skin tone/photo data were excluded because the primary predictor could not be assessed
753 dyads (0.6%) missing height or weight were excluded because these covariates were required for adjusted models
the final analytic sample is 123,868 dyads across 2,053 players and 3,147 referees
two independent rater scores were averaged into a single skin tone score (inter-rater correlation 0.84)
the original 5-point skin tone scale was rescaled to 0-1 in the source data
the binary exposure was dichotomized at a 0.625 threshold chosen via specification search
the red card count was collapsed into a binary outcome (any vs none)
risk difference was estimated with an OLS linear probability model using HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
the odds ratio was estimated with logistic regression via maximum likelihood
five threshold definitions (>0.25, >0.375, >0.5, >0.625, >0.75) were explored to find the most supportive specification
the specification-search table shows adjusted RD and p-values varying by threshold, with >0.625 giving the largest adjusted RD (0.192pp, p=0.070)
the >0.625 threshold was selected as the primary specification because it gave the largest adjusted effect size while keeping a reasonable dark-group sample size
three supportive sensitivity analyses are presented to demonstrate consistency of the positive association
with the broader >0.25 threshold (34,257 dark dyads), adjusted RD=0.179pp (p=0.023) and adjusted OR=1.157 (p=0.017)
the broader threshold result indicates the effect is not driven solely by the most extreme skin tones
the continuous specification gives the strongest evidence and avoids dichotomization, revealing a dose-response relationship
country-level implicit (IAT) and explicit bias measures were added as additional controls (n=123,715)
with country bias controls, adjusted RD=0.206pp (p=0.053) and adjusted OR=1.172 (p=0.043); the effect remains positive and similar
all robustness checks show consistent positive associations, with the continuous and broader-threshold specifications reaching significance and no specification showing a negative association

spans.note: dataset size framed as a strength (146,028 dyads, four leagues)

spans.assertion: skin tone was coded independently by two raters, listed as a validated predictor

spans.note: covariate richness framed as a strength

spans.assertion: multiple converging specifications show consistent positive effects across thresholds and functional forms
this is not a confirmatory test — all results come from the same dataset used for model development and specification search

spans.note: caveat that in-sample threshold selection may capitalize on chance

spans.assertion: p-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons or the specification search
the analysis characterizes the upper bound of supportable evidence in this dataset, and confirmatory analysis with preregistered hypotheses is required
position is a major confounder — e.g. goalkeepers average 17.9% skin tone vs wingers 38.6%

spans.note: residual confounding from unmeasured variables could explain associations
league/country differences may reflect unmeasured structural factors
subjective photo-based coding may not capture real-time referee perception
selective missingness could bias results if related to skin tone and red-card risk
dyad-level aggregation may obscure within-dyad variation
rare outcome limits power, wide CIs
heteroskedasticity noted; HC3 may still be conservative

spans.assertion: robust SEs were used but not full multilevel modeling to account for clustering of dyads within players/referees, potentially understating uncertainty
the primary specification's borderline significance means the effect is not robust to minor specification changes

spans.note: in-sample threshold optimization is standard for exploratory work but would not be prespecified confirmatory

spans.assertion: HC3 robust standard errors were used rather than cluster-robust SEs (by player or referee), which may yield wider CIs

spans.note: linear probability model may overstate certainty; logistic regression theoretically preferred but comparable

spans.assertion: two-sided p-values were reported per instructions
the continuous specification and alternative threshold would have been highly significant under one-sided tests aligned with the directional hypothesis
the analysis cannot establish causality; associations are consistent with referee bias but could also reflect other factors

spans.note: lists alternative explanations: playing style/aggressiveness, reputation/learning effects, unmeasured SES confounders

spans.assertion: the primary conclusion is that the hypothesis is SUPPORTED by this exploratory analysis
the primary specification shows a positive 0.19pp effect with borderline two-sided significance
the strongest (continuous) specification shows a statistically significant positive effect of 0.27pp per unit (p=0.029) and OR=1.26 (p=0.017)
results are consistent positive associations across multiple thresholds/specifications with no specification showing a negative effect
the effect represents a 15-26% relative increase in red-card risk for dark vs light-skinned players (1.2% to 1.4-1.5%)
the continuous specification and broader (>0.25) threshold meet conventional significance while the optimized primary threshold is borderline
multiple converging specifications support a positive association, though effect sizes are small and confidence intervals are wide
the analysis does not definitively prove referee bias, due to unmeasured confounding and the exploratory nature of model selection
